query: Which material can be used for improve the magnetocaloric properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, controlled amount of interstitial nitrogen into an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy will enhance its magnetocaloric properties compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy with a random solid solution structure
generation.intervention: Interstitially dope the alloy with nitrogen at controlled concentrations
generation.conditions: Ambient pressure and temperatures near the alloy’s magnetic transition (Curie) temperature, under the application of moderate magnetic fields
generation.structural_mediator: Interstitial nitrogen atoms that modify the lattice parameters and local atomic environments
generation.mechanism: The added nitrogen is expected to induce subtle lattice expansions and local electronic variations that alter magnetic exchange interactions. These changes may broaden or sharpen the magnetic phase transition, thereby increasing the magnetic entropy change (a key metric of the magnetocaloric effect).
generation.predicted_outcome: The nitrogen-doped CoCrFeMnNi HEA will exhibit a larger, more tunable magnetocaloric effect (i.e., a higher magnetic entropy change and/or improved adiabatic temperature change) around its Curie temperature when compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.boundary: The enhancement is expected to be sensitive to the precise nitrogen concentration and microstructural homogeneity; excessive doping or phase separation may negate the desired tuning of magnetic interactions.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of interstitial atoms in modifying physical properties of HEAs is supported by the literature, specific effects on magnetocaloric behavior in this system remain to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples with varying nitrogen doping levels (including an undoped control). Characterize the microstructure via XRD and electron microscopy to ensure phase homogeneity, then measure magnetization as a function of temperature and magnetic field. Calculate the magnetic entropy change (ΔS_m) and adiabatic temperature change (ΔT_ad) near the expected Curie temperature for each composition.
measurements: Magnetization vs. temperature and field measurements
Derived magnetic entropy change (ΔS_m) and adiabatic temperature change (ΔT_ad)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrogen-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in ΔS_m or ΔT_ad in comparison with the undoped sample—or if nitrogen doping leads to undesirable phase separations that degrade magnetocaloric performance—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
